items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: Not all reactions that have to be heated are endothermic reactions. Sometimes we just heat something to make it go faster.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 19.8 An endothermic change

items.label: text
items.text: needs to be absorbed from the surroundings. This heat energy is converted to chemical energy (energy stored in the bonds of chemicals). The temperature of the reaction mixture and the surroundings goes down because heat energy has been converted into a different form of energy.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 19.7 In an endothermic reaction, heat energy is converted to chemical energy. Heat is absorbed so the temperature goes down.

items.label: text
items.text: You have seen the thermal decomposition of metal carbonates before in Chapter 13. These are examples of endothermic reactions. You have to heat a carbonate constantly to make it decompose.

items.label: text
items.text: For example, copper(ll) carbonate (green) decomposes on heating to produce copper(ll) oxide (black).

items.label: formula
items.text: C u C O _ { 3 } ( s ) \rightarrow C u O ( s ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g )

items.label: text
items.text: Similarly, zinc carbonate decomposes to form zinc oxide when heated.

items.label: formula
items.text: Z n C O _ { 3 } ( s ) \to Z n O ( s ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g )

items.text: CHEMISTRY ONLY

items.label: section_header
items.text: SHOWING AN ENDOTHERMIC CHANGE ON AN ENERGY LEVEL DIAGRAM

items.label: text
items.text: In an endothermic change, the products have more energy than the reactants so we say that the products are less stable than the reactants. That extra energy has to come from somewhere, and it is taken from the surroundings. In the case of the thermal decomposition of carbonates in the laboratory, it comes from the Bunsen burner.

items.label: text
items.text: Because the reactants are gaining energy, the enthalpy change of the reaction ∆H is given a positive sign.

items.label: text
items.text: For example:

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } ( s ) \rightarrow C a O ( s ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g ) \quad \Delta H = + 1 7 8 \, k J / m o l

items.label: text
items.text: This means that 178 kJ of heat energy must be absorbed to convert 1 mole of calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

items.text: END OF CHEMISTRY ONLY

items.text: MEASURING ENTHALPY CHANGES OF REACTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: Here we discuss how we can measure how much heat is taken in or given out by a chemical reaction, in other words the enthalpy change of a reaction.
